title: processkit-cli `--error-format json` failure envelope
description: The single JSON line printed to **stderr** when an invocation run with the global `--error-format json` fails after parsing. Exactly one object per failed invocation, on stderr and never on stdout, so a command that printed a machine-readable report before failing (`probe --json`, `inspect --all --json`) leaves stdout byte-for-byte unchanged. `code` and `kind` carry the decision; `message` is explanatory only and is deliberately not pinned by the golden fixture. clap's parse-time usage errors (exit 100) stay human-readable in v1 — that boundary, and the `processkit-cli: warning: …` lines that are not failures at all, are stated in docs/exit-codes.md, "What the envelope does not cover". The normative prose is docs/exit-codes.md, "Machine-readable failures: `--error-format json`", and docs/integration.md §7; the in-code source of truth is src/error_envelope.rs. Validated against fixtures/schema/cli/error.jsonl, and against the real binary's stderr, by tests/machine_output.rs; its behavior (the flag's position independence, the unchanged default prose, and the kinds no fixture line pins) is covered by tests/error_envelope.rs.

errorEnvelope.description: One failed invocation. Bounded by construction: seven fields, every one of them a scalar — no nesting, no arrays, one line.

error_version.description: The envelope's own format version (src/error_envelope.rs, ERROR_VERSION) — an axis of its own, independent of the JSONL `schema_version`, the control-plane `snapshot_version`, the `registry_version`, and the probe report's `probe_version`. Pinned with `const` rather than enumerated as a range because this binary only ever *writes* an envelope, never reads one, so it has no tolerance window to express (contrast `inspect.schema.json`'s `snapshot_version`, which the client acts on). Bumped only by a breaking change to this shape; a new field, or a new `kind` value, is additive and does not bump it.

code.description: The reserved-band exit code this invocation exits with — the same number the process returns, so `$?` and the envelope can never disagree. See docs/exit-codes.md for the band and each code's meaning.

kind.description: What actually failed — a finer axis over `code`, never a competing one, and never coarser than it: `control_unreachable`/`not_found`/`stale`/`unprobed`/`ambiguous_run_id`/`ipc_deadline`/`incompatible_contract` all split CONTROL (103), and `registry` splits SETUP (111) away from every other prerequisite failure. The `run` family's values (`spawn_error`, `container_error`, `timeout`, `cancelled`, `control_cancel`, `control_kill`, `output_overflow`, `setup`, `internal`) are the terminal `runner_exit` event's `source` values, spelled identically: fixtures/schema/v1/schema.json's `runnerExit.source` remains their single source of truth and this envelope mirrors rather than forks that vocabulary. The list grows additively (a new value is a minor change); a reader that meets one it does not know falls back to `code`, which is always present. `unknown` is that fallback from this binary's own side — a reserved-band code this build will not name here, either because no build assigns it yet (the retired 105, the reserved 115-119) or because this build assigns it to a different subcommand than the one reporting (110/112/114 are minted only by probe/wait/events --validate, so a `run --detach` relaying one from a respawned copy that turned out to be a different build reports `unknown` rather than borrowing that meaning; src/run/detach.rs, `relayed_kind`).

operation.description: The subcommand that failed, spelled exactly as on the command line. Derived from the CLI definition itself (src/cli/mod.rs, `Command::name`), never from caller-supplied text, so it is always one of this closed set; a future subcommand joins it as an additive change.

run_id.description: The run id the invocation named, or null when it named none: an `--all` fan-out (whose targets are a snapshot, not one id), a whole-registry command (`list`/`prune`), the self-contained `probe`, or a `run` that let the runner generate its id — a generated id is minted inside the run and is not knowable at this point, so null is the truthful answer rather than a guess. Always present rather than omitted, so a consumer never has to distinguish absent from unknown.

retryable.description: Whether repeating this exact invocation, unchanged, may succeed later without the caller changing anything. A pure function of `kind` (src/error_envelope.rs, `ErrorKind::retryable`), so the two fields can never disagree — an adapter may equally well keep its own copy of the table. True for exactly three kinds: `unprobed` (nothing was established, so a second probe may establish something), `ipc_deadline` (a live runner was merely slower than a bounded window), and `wait_timeout` (the run is still live and untouched, so waiting again is the intended response). False is conservative — it means this build does not promise a retry helps, not that the condition is provably permanent — and every `run`-family kind is false on purpose: re-running a command is a new run with new side effects, not a retry of a read-only query.

message.description: The human-readable explanation — the very text the default prose mode prints after `processkit-cli: `. **Explicitly not part of the stable contract**: free to be reworded, re-punctuated, or made more specific in any release, which is why fixtures/schema/cli/error.jsonl replaces it with a fixed sample instead of pinning it. Log it, show it to a human, attach it to a ticket; never branch on it. Control characters are escaped by the JSON encoder rather than stripped, so the line is always exactly one line.

then.description: The three retryable kinds, pinned so the derived flag cannot drift from the vocabulary it is derived from.

else.description: Every other kind reports no retry advice.

then.description: The kinds that exist to split CONTROL (103) always carry that code. `registry` is deliberately absent from this list — it is the one kind reachable under two codes, CONTROL (103) when a by-`run-id` control client cannot resolve its target because the registry itself is unreadable, and SETUP (111) when a whole-registry command hits the same condition.
Only `wait` has a deadline of its own, and it is never the run's TIMEOUT (106) — see docs/exit-codes.md, "A waiter's deadline is not a run's deadline".
A verdict about a document, produced only by `events --validate`.
A pre-launch verdict about this binary: no run is involved, so there is no run id to name. The concrete unmet expectations are in `probe --json`'s own `mismatches` array on stdout.
These three take no `--run-id` at all, so they can never name one.
